request.state:
Subject: Re: [ILUG] OLPC & "third world" [was: Asus Eee PC ]

Timothy Murphy wrote:
> On Tue 30 Oct 2007, Josef Assad wrote:
> I don't agree.
> The OLPC seems to have several advantages,
> eg energy-efficient, hardy (because it uses a flash disk), etc,
> as well of course as being a laptop, and cheap.
> 
> I doubt if my Mac Plus would be found very useful in Niger.

Why would a computer have to be more hardy simply because it's intended
for an LDC?

Power consumption. That's a concern in rural areas of course.

Thing is, when one considers bang for development buck, urban areas
often provide the low-hanging fruit. I know that doesn't really help
with other development challenges like urban-rural migration, but how
many problems can you solve all at once?

I can only speak for the Arab region (been regional IT specialist for a
larger non-profit); I don't think power consumption is always one of the
key issues. For the same effort and cost outlays, you can accomplish
more in  urban or semi-urban environments than you can in rural ones.

Power efficiency further is less of a concern when electricity is cheap
enough (as it tends to be in LDCs, leastwise the ones I have worked in)
but where actual availability of electricity or a reliable current is
the real question mark. Further reducing the potential stature of power
consumption as a promotional factor for these devices, again most of the
markets I've seen (about 8 or 9 countries so far) get by with "stealing"
electricity. This is pervasive enough that I know of at least one UN
project (involving Linux desktops no less) where the schoolmaster
himself rigged up a discreet cable to a nearby electricity box.

The single isolated advantage I see to OLPC-type devices is that they
can be taken home. Can't do that with a clunky desktop. But, if it's
impact which is used as a measure for development work, then going out
and building a new device, new market channels, a new OS, a new GUI,
etc. isn't effective at all. If it's "whizbang-iness" which decides how
ICT4D is assessed, then of course Negroponte is on the right path.

Which, come to think of it, could explain a lot. A project to create an
efficient refurbished computer market doesn't sound half as sexy as a
whole new way of computing to donors.

'scuse the rambling...
